title: How I achieved consistent pixel art and fluid animations for my first AI-assisted survival game with Gemini and PixelLab
author: Ren9_3Dprinting
selftext:
Hey everyone,  
I just released my first game I made using AI on itch.io. It's an isometric survival game using pixel art sprites. Which brought a few hurdles with it. On the one hand there is the danger of having inconsistent characters, especially when they are animated and move in different directions, sleep, gather resources across the island and so on. Especially as I wanted to make my own characters and not use whatever the AI hands to me. But better begin at the start of the development.

While I was working on a non AI game for quite a while now, it just hit me. Why not try out AI gamedev for once. You know, just a small project. A game that builds itself and only takes a few days or a week at max. So I started by doing some ideation and came up with something that sounded like this:   
'The game revolves around a group of people washed ashore a lonely island after a shipwreck. An island far far away with no immediate rescue in sight. The player controls the main character and there are other characters he can order to do different tasks and so on.'

I wanted the game to be hard and punishing, consitently fighting for their survival and permadeath if somebody doesn't make it. In addition to that I added dating to the game... Which brings me to an important aspect of the game: characters, or more so pixel art characters. So how did I manage, previously coming from 3D to make consistent art?

First of all the AI did actually manage to create something that didn't look bad, but with no direction and the charactes where just placeholder cones. So, after looking a bit around I found a website called PixelLab, which has different tools to help with the creation of full automated pixel art. My condolences to all the proper pixel artists out there, because this is as good as it gets. I used it to create different things for the game, like ground tiles or objects, but the most important one was characters. Besides an editor called pixelorama there is also an editor that can automatically edit your pixel art, for example if you want your character to wear a hat you can do that via prompt.

https://i.redd.it/n5dsfkkgp64i1.png

But the tool I ended up using the most was a tab simply called characters. Here I created all of the characters for my game, the important ones that are dateable called Flames, where I put in some extra effort to give them some personality and make them look extra good. And a handful of characters that are in the game to do tasks like foraging called Sparks (the ones with a somewhat different style).  


After some back and fourth until getting the characters i wanted, I could just add the animations I needed with a few click directly on the page of the character. By the way, here's a tip when creating characters in pixellab. Before using pro mode for character generation, test out how they look with the cheaper V3 mode which only costs 3 generations (compared to 8 generations in pro mode at 128p). So animations can be created directly on the page of the respective character, just click add a state like walking, attacking, sleeping etc and then click on the direction you want and thats it.

https://i.redd.it/c03kvuyzu64i1.gif

The one thing that took some time was finding the style the characters in my game should have. First of all I went with 128p characters which have a more modern style to them with more details (there is an option for low and high detail, which influences the look besides the pixel dimension). And I also added cel shading to the desciption. After I got some characters that looked alright, I used them as style guide for new characters, which lets you decide which aspects of the character should appear similar (color palette, outline, detail and shading). Unfortunately the characters always end up having the same proportions as the guide, so be sure to use one with the body type your going for. I hope that gets fixed in the future. It's also important to choose the persective the character is seen in, like high or low top down for rpg maker type and all other isometric games or the other is sidescroller.  
  
Besides that I ended up being pretty satisfied with the results I got and ease of use as well as the consisteny in style after tinkering around for some time with character creation. In combination with gemini (or similar chatbots) I ended up making a fully working, not ai looking pixel art game called 'DATE & SURVIVE ISLAND'. So all characters, tiles and most objects were made with PixelLab, while a few where directly created with the ai (gemini). The thing however is, while it only took a few hours making a working game (where some people would call it a day), it took me around two weeks to make proper changes and create a game that isn't generic and doesn't only have the purpose of functioning or trying to look like an actual game. But maybe I will make a separate post about it, as this is way too long already.
